    Important Words
    • apakva-yoginaḥ — of an immature yogī
      Apakva = unripe, unbaked. Gauḍīyas use this same word in Caitanya-caritāmṛta to mark stages of bhakti — apakva śraddhā ripens into ruci, then bhāva, then prema. Yoga is no different: ripening, not declaring, is the criterion.
    • cittam — the mind
      Citta — the reflective mind, the locus of vāsanā. The yoga-sūtras define yoga as citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ; Gauḍīyas re-aim that nirodha toward Kṛṣṇa, not toward emptiness.
    • kāma-aktam — smeared with lust
      Compound: kāma (desire) + akta (anointed, smeared). Lust as a stain — not merely a thought but a tincture. Gauḍīyas know it is replaced not by suppression but by śuddha-kāma (Rādhā's kind) — the same energy, retargeted on Kṛṣṇa.
    • guṇa-yuk — joined with the modes
      Compound: guṇa + yuk (joined). The mind under guṇa's influence. The verse contrasts implicitly with the sthitaprajña of Gītā 2 — the mind no longer guṇa-yuk.
    • sindhuḥ — the ocean
      Sindhu — the great waters. In Vaiṣṇava imagery the ocean is also Viṣṇu's bed (Kṣīrodakaśāyī); the agitation here is not of the bed itself but of the meeting-point. The Lord rests; the conditioned mind churns.
    Where the rivers joined the ocean it became agitated, its waves blown about by the wind, just as the mind of an immature yogī becomes agitated because he is still tainted by lust and attached to the objects of sense gratification.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Where the rivers joined the ocean it became agitated, its waves blown about by the wind, just as the mind of an immature yogī becomes agitated because he is still tainted by lust and attached to the objects of sense gratification.
    Commentary

    The Sindhu river mixing with the smaller rivers becomes disturbed with turbulent waves. The use of masculine gender for sindhu instead of feminine is traditional usage. The desires in the yogi’s heart (kamasktam) are compared to the waves. The desires arise from the contact with the material objects (guna yuk), just as the waves arise from the merging of the smaller rivers.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    There is mention of the ocean, though it does not exist in Vṛndāvana, in order to describe the nature of the monsoon. However the word ocean can be taken as “like the ocean.” There is a huge lake called Koṭara, with power like Mānasa-gaṅgā, at the western edge of Mathurā district.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Where rivers fall into the ocean, the wind churns the meeting into agitation — like an immature yogī's mind where sense-objects still pour in and lust still blows. The mature yogī's mind is the Yamunā at midnight in Vraja: rivers entering without disturbance, because the centre is held by Kṛṣṇa's flute. Stillness is not the absence of inflow; it is the presence of the right Lord at the centre.

    Important Words
    • adhokṣaja-cetasaḥ — those whose minds are absorbed in the Lord beyond sense-perception
      Compound: Adhokṣaja (Bhagavān, beyond the senses' reach) + cetas (mind). Adhokṣaja is one of Viṣṇu's standing names — emphasizing His transcendence even as He is intimately reached by bhakti. Gauḍīyas treasure it as a precise anti-Māyāvāda term.
    • girayaḥ — the mountains
      Plural. Mountain-symbolism in the Bhāgavatam runs through Govardhana, Mandara, Trikūṭa. All bear the Lord; all are unmoved. The image is the standing emblem of dhairya (steadiness).
    • varṣa-dhārābhiḥ — by the streams of rain
      Compound: varṣa (rain) + dhārā (stream). The constant downpour of disturbances. Gauḍīyas note that the test is not occasional — it is continuous and is meant to be.
    • na vivyathuḥ — they were not agitated
      Negated aorist of vi + √vyath — to tremble. Trembling is precisely what a devotee does NOT do when the Lord is held in mind (cf. Gītā 6.22 — yaṁ labdhvā cāparaṁ lābhaṁ manyate).
    • vyasanaiḥ — by calamities
      Vyasana — distress, calamity. In Kuntī's prayer (SB 1.8.25), she asks for vipadaḥ because they bring Kṛṣṇa-darśana. Here the verse simply names what the devotee endures without trembling.
    Just as devotees whose minds are absorbed in the Personality of Godhead remain peaceful even when attacked by all sorts of dangers, the mountains in the rainy season were not at all disturbed by the repeated striking of the rain-bearing clouds.
    Purport

    When splashed by torrents of rain, the mountains are not shaken; rather, they are cleansed of dirt and become resplendent and beautiful. Similarly, an advanced devotee of the Supreme Lord is not shaken from his devotional program by disturbing conditions, which instead cleanse his heart of the dust of attachment to this world. Thus the devotee becomes beautiful and resplendent by tolerating difficult conditions. In fact, a devotee accepts all reverses in life as the mercy of Lord Kṛṣṇa, realizing that all suffering is due to the sufferer’s own previous misdeeds.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Just as devotees whose minds are absorbed in the Personality of Godhead remain peaceful even when attacked by all sorts of dangers, the mountains in the rainy season were not at all disturbed by the repeated striking of the rain-bearing clouds.
    Commentary

    Though struck by torrents of water, the mountain does not shake, but rather becomes beautiful, being washed of dirt. The devotee afflicted by pains caused by body, mind or other entities is not disturbed because his mind is absorbed in the Lord (adhoksaja citta). Bhagavatam says: material pains cannot disturb the devotee absorbed in me 3.25.23. Rather, that devotee remains free of pride envy and other bad qualities because of his humble attitude. Such difficulties are welcomed by the devotee.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Mountains struck by intense showers of rain, as if trying to defeat it (abhibhūyamānā), do not feel grief (vivyathuḥ) but rather become beautiful, being cleansed of dirt. Similarly a person thinking of the Lord does not grieve because of difficulties like sickness, since he must necessarily experience them as prārabdha-karma. Tvāṁ sevatāṁ sura-kṛtā bahavo ’ntarāyāḥ: the devatās place many obstacles on the path of those who worship you. (SB 11.8.10) Though being assaulted, the devotees do not feel grief. Rather they become glorious since they perfect remembrance of the Lord with the dissolving of bad karmas. That is indicated in Śrīdhara Svāmī’s commentary by the word eva: those who think of the Lord only are not disturbed by difficulties.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Mountains stand unmoved while rain-clouds beat them again and again — like a devotee whose mind is fixed on Adhokṣaja, undisturbed by every kind of danger. Gauḍīyas hear this line as Prahlāda's posture in advance. The mountain does not negotiate with the cloud; it lets the cloud pour itself out on its slope.

    Stories
    Prahlāda untouched by every weapon

    Hiraṇyakaśipu tried fire, poison, snakes, mystic missiles, elephants — and Prahlāda, five years old, was not disturbed (SB 7.5). His body was where the rains struck; his mind was on the Lord beyond senses (Adhokṣaja). The verse's mountain is Prahlāda made geological.

    Gauḍīyas use this pair — verse and story — as the picture of mind-fixedness. Outer storms test only the surface; the inner peak is held by Kṛṣṇa.

    Govardhana itself, soon to come

    Two chapters ahead in this very canto, Kṛṣṇa will lift Govardhana while Indra's clouds beat it for seven days. The mountain in SB 10.20.15 is foreshadowing — its unmoved stance, when the time comes, is literally Kṛṣṇa's hand.

    Gauḍīya tradition reads chapter 20 and chapters 24–25 as one arc. The mountain holds because Kṛṣṇa holds it.

    Important Words
    • śrutayaḥ — the revealed scriptures
      Śruti — that which is heard, the Vedic revelation. The standing pramāṇa of all Hindu darśanas. Gauḍīyas read Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam itself as the natural commentary on śruti (artho 'yaṁ brahma-sūtrāṇām, SB 1.2.2 colophon).
    • dvijaiḥ — by the twice-born
      Dvija — twice-born; brāhmaṇa by samskāra. The śruti's natural keepers. Gauḍīyas note: when the keepers neglect, anyone — Haridāsa Ṭhākura (born Muslim), Rūpa-Sanātana (former Yavana-court officials) — can take up the burden by Kṛṣṇa's grace.
    • asaṁskṛtāḥ — uncleansed, unrefined
      Privative + sam + √kṛ — not refined, not prepared. The roads are asaṁskṛta; so are minds without sādhana. Saṁskāra is what makes both a road and a soul usable.
    • kālena — by time
      Instrumental of kāla. Time corrupts; only what is re-spoken survives. Gauḍīyas hear this and remember Mahāprabhu's harer nāma — the one thing time cannot grind down because it is re-spoken every moment by His devotees.
    • tṛṇaiḥ-channāḥ — covered with grass
      Tṛṇa (grass, weed) + channa (covered). Vivid image. Even sacred land returns to weed without traffic. Bhakti is the traffic that keeps the dhāma a dhāma.
    During the rainy season the roads, not being cleansed, became covered with grass and debris and were thus difficult to make out. These roads were like religious scriptures that brāhmaṇas no longer study and that thus become corrupted and covered over with the passage of time.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    During the rainy season the roads, not being cleansed, became covered with grass and debris and were thus difficult to make out. These roads were like religious scriptures that brāhmaṇas no longer study and that thus become corrupted and covered over with the passage of time.
    Commentary

    Not studying the scriptures is compared to the unclean paths. Scriptures being lost due to time is compared to the paths overgrown with grass. The scriptures and the path are both defiled. This is unfavorable for the brahmanas.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The roads are like the Vedas not being studied, destroyed by Kali-yuga. There is a version with śrutayaḥ iva and with kālena āhataḥ as well as kālena hatāḥ. The word iva means “and.”

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Untrodden, the rainy-season roads vanish under grass and litter — like śrutis that brāhmaṇas no longer chant. Scripture is not preserved by being kept on a shelf; it is preserved by being walked on, spoken aloud, taught. The remedy for Kali's overgrown roads is the saṅkīrtana of Mahāprabhu — feet and tongues simultaneously clearing the path.

    Stories
    Six Gosvāmīs recovering the lost places of Vraja

    When Caitanya sent Rūpa and Sanātana to Vṛndāvana, the forest had grown over every līlā-sthala. They walked the ground inch by inch, identified Govardhana, Rādhā-kuṇḍa, Yāvaṭa, Nandagrāma — and wrote, sang, taught. The verse's overgrown roads describe the pre-Caitanya Vraja exactly; the Gosvāmīs are the verse's antidote.

    Gauḍīyas read SB 10.20.16 as a quiet prophecy: śrutis go unread, holy places go forgotten — until a saṅkīrtana-movement walks them back into use.

    Important Words
    • cala-sauhṛdāḥ — those of fickle friendship
      Compound: cala (moving, fickle) + sauhṛda (friendship). The opposite of the gopīs, whose sauhṛda toward Kṛṣṇa is sthira-tama — most steady. The verse implicitly contrasts worldly flicker with Vraja-fidelity.
    • loka-bandhuṣu — to the friends of the world (clouds)
      Compound: loka (world) + bandhu (kin, friend). Clouds are loka-bandhu by their universal mercy. Kṛṣṇa is the ultimate loka-bandhu (cf. Gītā 5.29 — suhṛdaṁ sarva-bhūtānām).
    • sthairyam — steadiness
      From √sthā — to stand. Sthairya is a quality of the mature bhakta (cf. Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu — sthāyī-bhāva is steady, not fleeting). The lightning's lack of sthairya is the diagnosis the verse offers.
    • guṇiṣu — to virtuous men
      Locative plural of guṇin — possessed of guṇa (here, virtue, not material mode). The verse plays on guṇa's double sense, which Gauḍīyas always note: the same word names material mode and spiritual quality, distinguished by context.
    • vidyutaḥ — the lightning
      Nominative plural — the various lightning-flashes. Each one fickle. The Bhāgavatam often uses lightning to indicate something flashing but not lasting; gold ornaments on Kṛṣṇa are vidyut-stable, lightning in clouds is not.
    Though the clouds are the well-wishing friends of all living beings, the lightning, fickle in its affinities, moved from one group of clouds to another, like lusty women unfaithful even to virtuous men.
    Purport

    Śrīla Prabhupāda comments: “During the rainy season, lightning appears in one group of clouds and then immediately in another group of clouds. This phenomenon is compared to a lusty woman who does not fix her mind on one man. A cloud is compared to a qualified person because it pours rain and gives sustenance to many people; a man who is qualified similarly gives sustenance to many living creatures, such as family members or many workers in business. Unfortunately, his whole life can be disturbed by a wife who divorces him; when the husband is disturbed, the whole family is ruined, the children are dispersed or the business is closed, and everything is affected. It is therefore recommended that a woman desiring to advance in Kṛṣṇa consciousness peacefully live with a husband and that the couple not separate under any condition. The husband and wife should control sex indulgence and concentrate their minds on Kṛṣṇa consciousness so their life may be successful. After all, in the material world a man requires a woman and a woman requires a man. When they are combined, they should live peacefully in Kṛṣṇa consciousness and should not be restless like the lightning, flashing from one group of clouds to another.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Though the clouds are the well-wishing friends of all living beings, the lightning, fickle in its affinities, moved from one group of clouds to another, like lusty women unfaithful even to virtuous men.
    Commentary

    Though a man may have good qualities such as intelligence, he cannot hold a prostitute’s attention for long. Similarly the lightening does not remain for long with the cloud. This is a negative analogy.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Lusty women are not steady attached to even the men may be endowed with good qualities like grace.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Lightning, fickle, flits from cloud to cloud, never settling on one host — like an unfaithful woman among virtuous men. The verse uses an unsparing simile to name an old human disease: the heart that cannot stay. Gauḍīya bhakti is the cure precisely as ekāgratā — one-pointedness — fixed on Kṛṣṇa alone, never flickering.

    Important Words
    • nirguṇam — without (material) qualities
      Nir + guṇa. Gauḍīyas distinguish carefully: nirguṇa means free of material guṇas, not devoid of all attributes. Kṛṣṇa is nirguṇa (no material modes) yet sa-viśeṣa (full of transcendental qualities) — against Māyāvāda's attributeless absolute.
    • guṇa-vyatikare — in the interaction of the modes
      Compound: guṇa + vyatikara (mixing, interaction). The world as the churn of the three guṇas. Kṛṣṇa enters this churn as Avatāra without being shaped by it — the doctrine of svarūpa-rakṣā, preservation of His own form.
    • aguṇa-vān — one who is free of (material) qualities
      A + guṇa + possessive suffix vān — strictly, 'possessed of no-qualities,' meaning free of material modes. The verse pairs aguṇa-vān (the Lord) with guṇa-vyatikara (the world). Acintya-bhedābheda condensed.
    • māhā-indram — Indra's great bow
      Indra's bow = the rainbow. In Vaiṣṇava reading the rainbow is also a memento of Indra's eventual humbling by Kṛṣṇa under Govardhana — a few chapters away. The bow without a string belongs structurally to one greater than Indra.
    • puruṣaḥ — the Supreme Person
      Puruṣa — the Person. The verse's punch-line: He is Person, He enters the world, He stays Himself. Gauḍīyas refuse to dilute puruṣa to 'principle' or 'consciousness'; He is Kṛṣṇa.
    When the curved bow of Indra [the rainbow] appeared in the sky, which had the quality of thundering sound, it was unlike ordinary bows because it did not rest upon a string. Similarly, when the Supreme Lord appears in this world, which is the interaction of the material qualities, He is unlike ordinary persons because He remains free from all material qualities and independent of all material conditions.
    Purport

    Śrīla Prabhupāda comments as follows: “Sometimes, in addition to the roaring thunder of the clouds, there is an appearance of a rainbow, which stands as a bow without a string. Actually, a bow is in the curved position because it is tied at its two ends by the bowstring; but in the rainbow there is no such string, and yet it rests in the sky so beautifully. Similarly, when the Supreme Personality of Godhead descends to this material world, He appears just like an ordinary human being, but He is not resting on any material condition. In the Bhagavad-gītā, the Lord says that He appears by His internal potency, which is free from the bondage of the external potency. What is bondage for the ordinary creature is freedom for the Personality of Godhead.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the curved bow of Indra [the rainbow] appeared in the sky, which had the quality of thundering sound, it was unlike ordinary bows because it did not rest upon a string. Similarly, when the Supreme Lord appears in this world, which is the interaction of the material qualities, He is unlike ordinary persons because He remains free from all material qualities and independent of all material conditions.
    Commentary

    Just as the Lord, though without material gunas (agunavan) appears in the material world to perform pastimes, so the rainbow without a string (nirguna) appears in the akasa, which has the quality of sound (gunini). (This is a play on words.)

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord is beyond the guṇas of māyā (aguṇavān). Thus he is called the puruṣaḥ, he who controls māyā. The world is manifested by the guṇas of māyā. Paramātmā appears in the world (vyakte) made of material guṇas as the giver of consciousness, without guṇas (aguṇavān), just as the rainbow appears in the sky without its string (nirguṇam). Or the Lord appears in the world with his qualities like mercy (guṇa-vyatikare). Or the Lord who is without the qualities of the jīva (aguṇavaṇ) since he is Brahman manifests through acts like hearing about the Lord (guṇa-vyaktikare). Or Kṛṣṇa manifests in Vṛndāvana, his famous place (vyakte) in which there is a mixture of spiritual qualities (guṇa-vyatikare).

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The rainbow appears in the cloud-thundering sky without a string — a bow with no string is Kṛṣṇa's signature. He enters guṇa-vyatikara as the rainbow enters the cloud: present, visible, untouched by the materials He uses. Mādhurya-yet-aiśvarya is the rainbow.

    Stories
    Rāma's bow and Indra's bow

    When Rāma broke Śiva's bow in the svayaṁvara hall (Bālakāṇḍa) and later strung the Kodaṇḍa for Khara's army, His weapons obeyed Him without being part of Him. The Bhāgavatam's rainbow image is the cosmic version — a bow that does not need a string because the Lord whose emblem it is needs no support.

    Gauḍīyas read SB 10.20.18 as a quiet teaching about avatāra: Kṛṣṇa uses guṇa as Rāma uses bow, without becoming what He uses.

    Important Words
    • aham-matyā — by the conception of 'I'
      Compound: aham (I) + mati (conception). Ahaṅkāra in its functional form — the working notion of self. Gauḍīyas distinguish śuddha-ahaṁ (kṛṣṇa-dāso 'smi) from material ahaṁ (this body is me). The cloud here is the second.
    • uḍupaḥ — the moon
      Uḍu-pa — lord of the stars. The moon as governor of the night sky. In Vraja-poetry the moon is also Kṛṣṇa's face (mukha-candra); the simile is layered.
    • sva-jyotsnā — with its own moonlight
      Compound: sva (own) + jyotsnā (moonlight). The clouds shine 'with the moon's own light' that they then conceal. A miniature of how māyā works — borrowing light from the spirit and then hiding the spirit.
    • puruṣaḥ — the spirit-soul
      Puruṣa here = the jīva (spirit-soul), as distinct from verse 18 where puruṣa is paramount Bhagavān. The same word; Gauḍīyas always read by context. Both are puruṣa; one is svatantra, the other paratantra.
    • channaḥ — covered
      Past participle of √chad — to cover. The standing term for the jīva's predicament. Bhakti uncovers; jñāna at best identifies the cover; karma rearranges its drapery.
    During the rainy season the moon was prevented from appearing directly by the covering of the clouds, which were themselves illumined by the moon’s rays. Similarly, the living being in material existence is prevented from appearing directly by the covering of the false ego, which is itself illumined by the consciousness of the pure soul.
    Purport

    The analogy given here is excellent. During the rainy season we cannot see the moon in the sky, because the moon is covered by clouds. These clouds, however, are radiant with the glow of the moon’s own rays. Similarly, in our conditioned, material existence we cannot directly perceive the soul, because our consciousness is covered by the false ego, which is the false identification with the material world and the material body. Yet it is the soul’s own consciousness that illumines the false ego. As the Gītā describes, the energy of the soul is consciousness, and when this consciousness manifests through the screen of false ego, it appears as dull, material consciousness, in which there is no direct vision of the soul or God. In the material world, even great philosophers ultimately resort to hazy ambiguities when speaking about the Absolute Truth, just as the cloudy sky manifests only in a dull and indirect way the iridescent light of the moon. In material life, our false ego is often enthusiastic, hopeful and apparently aware of various material affairs, and such consciousness encourages us to push on in material existence. But in truth we are merely experiencing the dull reflection of our original, pure consciousness, which is Kṛṣṇa consciousness — direct perception of the soul and God. Not realizing that the false ego merely hampers and dulls our real, spiritual consciousness, which is fully enlightened and blissful, we mistakenly think that material consciousness is full of knowledge and happiness. This is comparable to thinking that the luminous clouds are lighting up the night sky, while in fact it is the moonshine that illumines the sky, and the clouds that merely dull and hamper the moonshine. The clouds appear luminous because they are filtering and impeding the brilliant rays of the moon. Similarly, at times material consciousness appears pleasurable or enlightened because it is screening or filtering the original, blissful and enlightened consciousness coming directly from the soul. If we can understand the ingenious analogy given in this verse, we can easily advance in Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    During the rainy season the moon was prevented from appearing directly by the covering of the clouds, which were themselves illumined by the moon's rays. Similarly, the living being in material existence is prevented from appearing directly by the covering of the false ego, which is itself illumined by the consciousness of the pure soul.
    Commentary

    The moon does not shine, being covered by the mist which is itself illuminated by the moon, just as the Lord (purusa) is not visible, being hidden by his avidya sakti , which arises from himself. This is a good example for the jnanis.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The moon, covered by clouds which are revealed by the cool light of the moon, did not shine.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The clouds are lit by the moonlight, not the moon directly. The ahamkāra is lit by the light of the soul. This defeats the atheists’ proposal that the jīva is just prāṇa. The clouds are increased (rājitaiḥ) by the cool rays of the moon. This is the cause of the moon being covered. Similarly the jīva gets covered by ahaṁkāra. But the ahaṁkāra is revealed by the consciousness of the jīva. Or the moon covered by clouds does not shine by illumination of its rays. Since even the rays are covered, the moon cannot shine properly. Similarly the jīva, being covered by ahaṁkāra, does not shine (does not reveal its true nature), though illumined by its own consciousness.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The moon shines, the clouds shine because they catch its light, and yet the moon itself is hidden by them — like the pure ātmā illumining the false ego which then hides it. Gauḍīyas read the verse precisely: the jīva is a tiny moon, the false ego the cloud, and Kṛṣṇa the still-larger sun beyond both. The cloud cannot self-illumine; only by borrowed light does it shine at all.

    Important Words
    • acyuta-jana — people of the Infallible Lord
      Compound: Acyuta (Kṛṣṇa, the Infallible) + jana (people). The devotees of the Infallible One — an aiśvarya-tinted name for Bhaktas. Gauḍīyas note: Acyuta highlights the Lord's never-falling; His devotees inherit that quality through niṣṭhā.
    • śikhaṇḍinaḥ — the peacocks
      Śikhaṇḍa = crest. Kṛṣṇa Himself wears the śikhaṇḍa (peacock-crest) — śikhaṇḍa-cūḍa is one of His Vraja-names. The peacock is the verse's image and Kṛṣṇa's ornament: another Vraja-rhyme.
    • tapta-nirviṇṇāḥ — scorched and dejected
      Compound: tapta (scorched) + nirviṇṇa (disgusted, weary). The standard Bhāgavatam diagnosis of saṁsāra. Vairāgya begins as nirveda — this verse names it precisely.
    • megha-āgama — the arrival of clouds
      Compound: megha (cloud) + āgama (arrival). The verb āgama is later used for sādhu-saṅga and ācārya-darśana — sacred arrival in any key.
    • pratyanandan — they greeted joyfully
      Imperfect of prati + ā + √nand — to rejoice in return. The peacocks return joy to the clouds. Gauḍīyas read this as how welcoming a Vaiṣṇava works — not a passive reception but an active glad cry.
    The peacocks became festive and cried out a joyful greeting when they saw the clouds arrive, just as people distressed in household life feel pleasure when the pure devotees of the infallible Supreme Lord visit them.
    Purport

    After the dry summer season, the peacocks become jubilant with the arrival of the first thundering rain clouds, and thus they dance in great happiness. Śrīla Prabhupāda comments, “We have practical experience of this: many of our students were dry and morose previous to their coming to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, but having come into contact with devotees they are now dancing like jubilant peacocks.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The peacocks became festive and cried out a joyful greeting when they saw the clouds arrive, just as people distressed in household life feel pleasure when the pure devotees of the infallible Supreme Lord visit them.
    Commentary

    Happy to see the approaching clouds, hearing the rumbling of thunder, the peacocks begin to call loudly This is just like the vaisnava grhastha who after hearing the songs of the vaisnavas begins to sing and dance in bliss. This example is suitable for devotees.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The peacock, festive at the coming of clouds, and joyous, cried out after the clouds rumbled. Similarly devotee householders, after the arrival of devotees who sing, sing and dance themselves.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The peacocks become cheerful (utsavā) or perform acts like dancing when the clouds arrive. Joy (hṛṣtāḥ) is a transformation of that cheerfulness or its effect. The peacock, festive at the coming of clouds, and joyous, cried out and danced after the clouds rumbled. Similarly devotee householders, after the arrival of devotees who sing, sing and dance themselves. Or the peacocks at every moment (prati) were happy (anandan) just as householders become naturally happy when devotees arrive. Utsava, hṛṣṭāḥ and anandan express successive causes, from external to internal. The cātaka birds responded similarly but because their voices are plaintive they are not mentioned. Remembering them invokes sadness.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Peacocks cry with joy when the clouds come — exactly as householders crushed by gṛhastha-life rejoice when Vaiṣṇavas arrive at the door. The cloud and the sādhu carry the same gift: relief that has travelled a long way. Vraja's peacocks know first what the rest of the worlds slowly learn.

    Stories
    Citraketu welcoming Nārada and Aṅgirā

    When Citraketu, crushed by the death of his son, sat in palace darkness, Nārada and Aṅgirā walked in — and his grief began to lift before they spoke (SB 6.15). Like the peacock greeting the cloud, his heart cried out at the very sight of Vaiṣṇavas.

    Gauḍīyas read SB 10.20.20 as Citraketu's diagnosis: gṛheṣu tapta-nirviṇṇāḥ — those scorched and dejected in household life. The cure is acyuta-jana-āgama, the arrival of the Infallible's devotees.

    Important Words
    • kāma-anusevayā — by serving lust (sense-objects)
      Compound: kāma (desire) + anu-sevā (continual service). The man here serves his lust as a devotee serves the Lord — but with reversed phala. Gauḍīyas note: kāma-anusevā and hari-sevā are the two possible niṣṭhās of a human life.
    • pāda-pāḥ — the trees (drinkers-with-feet)
      Compound: pāda (foot, root) + pa (drinker). Sanskrit's lovely name for trees. Gauḍīyas use it in nāma-saṅgraha — trees drink with feet; devotees drink kṛpā with the lifted head and the bent foot at Kṛṣṇa's feet.
    • ātma-mūrtayaḥ — various bodily features
      Compound: ātmā (self/body) + mūrti (form). Here ātmā is used in its lower sense — body-self. Gauḍīyas always disambiguate: ātmā can mean body, mind, jīva, or paramātmā, depending on context.
    • tapasā — by austerity
      Instrumental of tapas. Three references to tapas in this chapter (vv. 7, 21, 38) trace the same arc: tapas without bhakti only re-fattens the body. Gauḍīyas use these verses to teach yukta-vairāgya.
    • kṣāmāḥ — thin, withered
      Past participle adjective — emaciated. Used for both trees and ascetics. The verse trusts the reader to feel the irony: emaciated by what — the summer, or one's own choices?
    The trees had grown thin and dry, but after they drank the newly fallen rainwater through their feet, their various bodily features blossomed. Similarly, one whose body has grown thin and weak from austerity again exhibits his healthy bodily features upon enjoying the material objects gained through that austerity.
    Purport

    The word pāda means foot, and pā means drinking. Trees are called pādapa because they drink through their roots, which are likened to feet. Upon drinking the newly fallen rainwater, the trees in Vṛndāvana began to manifest new leaves, sprouts and blossoms, and they thus enjoyed new growth. Similarly, materialistic persons often perform severe austerities to acquire the object of their desire. For example, politicians in America undergo grueling austerities while traveling about the countryside campaigning for election. Businessmen also will often deny personal comfort to make their business successful. Such austere persons, upon acquiring the fruits of their austerity, again become healthy and satisfied, like trees eagerly drinking rainwater after enduring the austerity of a dry, hot summer.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The trees had grown thin and dry, but after they drank the newly fallen rainwater through their feet, their various bodily features blossomed. Similarly, one whose body has grown thin and weak from austerity again exhibits his healthy bodily features upon enjoying the material objects gained through that austerity.
    Commentary

    As the trees become filled with various forms such as sprouts, leaves, and flowers during the rainy season, so the tapasvi, by enjoying material objects, nourishes him body. This of course is unfavorable for those practicing detachment.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Those who are thin and weak because of austerities take on various (healthy) features after enjoying objects. The trees in the summer, on drinking water, take on various features.

    Analogy

    Drinking through their feet, the dry trees flower again — but only after long thirst. The verse compares this to a man whose body, thinned by tapas, fills out again on its hard-won reward. Once more the Bhāgavatam quietly tilts the comparison: the trees' green is honest, the materialist's fattening on tapas-fruit is not.

    Important Words
    • durāśayāḥ — of polluted heart
      Compound: dur (bad) + āśaya (heart, intent). The standing diagnosis of the materialist in the Bhāgavatam. Gauḍīyas note: the cure is sat-saṅga, which slowly transforms āśaya from dur to su (good).
    • gṛheṣu — in households
      Locative plural of gṛha — house. Not gṛhastha-āśrama (a sacred station) but gṛhamedhī life (cf. SB 2.1.2 — śva-viḍ-varāhoṣṭra-kharaiḥ). Gauḍīyas read 'gṛheṣu' through this lens unless context says otherwise.
    • sārasāḥ — cranes
      Sārasa — the long-legged crane that haunts agitated shores. The bird that mistakes commotion for company. The Bhāgavatam's chosen image for one of the subtlest pitfalls.
    • aśānta — unpeaceful, disturbed
      A + śānta. The opposite of the śānta-rasa of the great Vaiṣṇavas. Gauḍīyas note: a long aśānta history is not a disqualification for bhakti — Ajāmila was aśānta and still went home.
    • grāmyāḥ — village-like, mundane
      Grāmya — pertaining to grāma (village), hence rustic, common, oriented to gṛhastha pleasures. A standing pejorative in Vaiṣṇava literature, used by Rūpa Gosvāmī to name the kind of conversation that pollutes bhakti.
    The cranes continued dwelling on the shores of the lakes, although the shores were agitated during the rainy season, just as materialistic persons with contaminated minds always remain at home, despite the many disturbances there.
    Purport

    During the rainy season there are often mud slides around the shores of lakes, and thorny bushes, stones and other debris sometimes accumulate there. Despite all these inconveniences, ducks and cranes continue meandering around the lakeshores. Similarly, innumerable painful occurrences are always disturbing family life, but a materialistic man never even considers leaving his family in the hands of his grown sons and going away for spiritual improvement. He regards such an idea as shocking and uncivilized, because he is completely ignorant of the Absolute Truth and his relationship to that Truth.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The cranes continued dwelling on the shores of the lakes, although the shores were agitated during the rainy season, just as materialistic persons with contaminated minds always remain at home, despite the many disturbances there.
    Commentary

    The cranes dwell intently on the lake shores, though littered with mud, thorns and weeds. This is similar to the materialistic person dwelling in the house in spite of so many disturbances there. This example is unfavorable.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The cranes constantly dwell (ni—ūsuḥ) on the banks of lakes disturbed constantly by huge waves. The bird sārasa is also called puṣkara. People with no intelligence (grāmyāḥ), who develop bad intentions (durāśayāḥ) because everything is provided in the house, constantly remain in their houses. Out of astonishment or sorrow, Śukadeva calls to Parīkṣit, “O king (aṅga)!”

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The cranes refuse to leave the agitated shore — like householders so accustomed to the chaos of home-life that the chaos itself becomes love. The verse names them durāśaya, of polluted heart. Gauḍīyas do not condemn gṛhastha-āśrama; they condemn the inability to perceive its disturbance and walk away when bhakti calls.

    Stories
    Bharata's deer, the disturbance he could not leave

    King Bharata, retired to the forest for bhakti, rescued an orphaned deer and slowly transferred his heart from Bhagavān to the fawn (SB 5.7–8). He could not leave the agitation he loved — and was reborn as a deer to learn the lesson. The cranes of this verse stand on a similar shore.

    Gauḍīyas use Bharata as the cautionary case: even one beloved disturbance, unrenounced, can pull a sādhaka through a whole janma. Better to take darśana and leave the shore.

    Important Words
    • pāṣaṇḍinām — of the atheists
      Genitive plural of pāṣaṇḍī. The same word as in v. 8 but now in agentive form. The pāṣaṇḍas are not just doctrines but persons; the Bhāgavatam is realistic about who breaks the dikes.
    • asat-vādaiḥ — by false arguments
      Compound: asat (unreal, false) + vāda (argument). Gauḍīyas use sat-vāda for any argument that converges on Kṛṣṇa as Bhagavān; asat-vāda is its opposite. The criterion is not eloquence but conclusion.
    • veda-mārgāḥ — paths of the Veda
      Compound: Veda + mārga (path). The varṇa-āśrama-prescriptions, the sacrificial paths, ultimately culminating in bhakti. Gauḍīyas treasure the Veda's paths as the natural staircase to Kṛṣṇa-prema.
    • setavaḥ — dikes, boundaries
      Setu — the same word used for Rāma's setu to Laṅkā. Boundaries are sacred in Vedic culture (cf. Manu's metaphors). To break a setu is a serious crime — physical, social, or hermeneutic.
    • kalau — in Kali (age)
      Locative. The age explicitly named in a verse about the rainy season — the poet uses every device to remind us that varṣā is also Kali in micro.
    When Indra sent forth his rains, the floodwaters broke through the irrigation dikes in the agricultural fields, just as in the Kali-yuga the atheists’ false theories break down the boundaries of Vedic injunctions.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When Indra sent forth his rains, the floodwaters broke through the irrigation dikes in the agricultural fields, just as in the Kali-yuga the atheists' false theories break down the boundaries of Vedic injunctions.
    Commentary

    Indra, thinking himself the Lord, pours down excessive rain and causes disturbance, as by the influence of Kali, the materialists destroy dharma. . Kali is compared to Indra, the activities of the materialists to the rains, and the destruction of vedic dharma to the destruction of dikes. This is an unfavorable example.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Indra is called īśvara to indicate his independent action of pouring rain. Similarly the atheists independently destroy the rules of the Vedas.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    When Indra rains hard, even the strongest dikes give way — and in Kali, pāṣaṇḍa-arguments break the dikes of Vedic injunction. The verse is bleak about the present age. Mahāprabhu's answer is to rebuild the dikes higher with nāma-saṅkīrtana — a project that does not depend on the dikes' brittle mud.

    Stories
    Mahāprabhu's debate with the Kazi

    When the Kazi of Navadvīpa banned kīrtana, Mahāprabhu led a torchlit procession to his door. The Kazi argued from his own scripture; Mahāprabhu argued from the Veda and from common reason — until the Kazi wept and joined the kīrtana himself (Caitanya-caritāmṛta, Ādi 17).

    Gauḍīyas read this as the corrective to SB 10.20.23. Dikes can be rebuilt; pāṣaṇḍas can be turned. The means is not stronger walls but stronger mercy in the heart of the saṅkīrtana-leader.

    Important Words
    • amṛtam — nectar
      Amṛta — deathless, nectarean. Rain is called amṛta when it is timely and pure. Gauḍīyas use the same word for Kṛṣṇa's nāma (nāmāmṛta) and for the wisdom of jñānī-Vaiṣṇavas (jñāna-amṛta, v. 36).
    • viṭ-patayaḥ — the lords of the people (kings)
      Compound: viṭ (Vaiśya/community/people) + pati (lord). Kings as keepers of the people, not as owners. Gauḍīyas always emphasize the dāsa-character of kingship in dharmic theory — the king serves Kṛṣṇa by serving the people.
    • dvija-īritāḥ — impelled by brāhmaṇas
      Compound: dvija (twice-born brāhmaṇa) + īrita (impelled, instructed). The proper sequence: brāhmaṇa instructs, kṣatriya executes. When inverted, Kali. Gauḍīyas trace many social failures to this inversion.
    • ghanāḥ — clouds
      Ghana — thick, dense. The dense clouds release amṛta. Density and depth are themes — what is shallow cannot give amṛta. The image returns in verse 36 with the mountains.
    • āśiṣaḥ — blessings
      Plural of āśīs — blessing. The water itself is called blessing. Gauḍīyas note: even physical resources, given through the right channels, are blessing; given through wrong channels, they are bondage.
    The clouds, impelled by the winds, released their nectarean water for the benefit of all living beings, just as kings, instructed by their brāhmaṇa priests, dispense charity to the citizens.
    Purport

    Śrīla Prabhupāda comments: “In the rainy season, the clouds, tossed by the wind, deliver water, which is welcomed like nectar. When the Vedic followers, the brāhmaṇas, inspire rich men like kings and the wealthy mercantile community to give charity in the performance of great sacrifices, the distribution of such wealth is also nectarean. The four sections of human society, namely the brāhmaṇas, the kṣatriyas, the vaiśyas and the śūdras, are meant to live peacefully in a cooperative mood; this is possible when they are guided by expert Vedic brāhmaṇas who perform sacrifices and distribute wealth equally.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The clouds, impelled by the winds, released their nectarean water for the benefit of all living beings, just as kings, instructed by their brāhmaṇa priests, dispense charity to the citizens.
    Commentary

    Just as a king or head merchant (vitpatayah) inspired by purohits (dvijeritah ) fulfils everyones desires (asisah), so the clouds, incited (nunna) by the winds, release rain. The analogy with the king is positive.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The word ca means again, after the incessant rains. Another version has atha with the same meaning. The clouds release rain at suitable times to the living beings. Rain is called amṛtam because it is most beneficial for them. Vyamuṣcan means the clouds released water for excellent purposes. The kings, directed by brāhmaṇas similarly release wealth.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The clouds released glorious water (amṛtam) for benefiting all living beings (bhūtebhyaḥ). Water at the end of the monsoon is precious. Vyamuṣcan means the clouds released water for excellent purposes. Ca can have the meaning “but.” But sometimes (kale kale) the clouds released water to the living beings. At the end of the monsoon the showers were not continuous. This verse is a more particular description of the showers than the previous one.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Wind-pushed clouds release nectarean water — like kings, instructed by brāhmaṇas, releasing charity. The verse names the proper political theology: rulers are clouds, brāhmaṇas are wind, jīvas drink the water. When kings ignore brāhmaṇas, the rains stop; when brāhmaṇas serve Kṛṣṇa, the rains are abundant and sweet.

    Stories
    Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya, with Kṛṣṇa as advisor

    At Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya sacrifice, the king distributed wealth so lavishly that it was said even Indra envied the rain of gold (Mahābhārata, Sabhā-parva). The structure was exact: brāhmaṇas instructed, the king dispensed, the people drank. Kṛṣṇa Himself sat in the council.

    Gauḍīyas read this as SB 10.20.24 in human form. A Vaiṣṇava king with brāhmaṇa-advisors and Kṛṣṇa at the centre is rain itself, walking the earth.

    Important Words
    • hariḥ — Lord Hari (Kṛṣṇa)
      Hari — He who removes (kleśa, ignorance, distance). Gauḍīyas relish Hari as an early name for Kṛṣṇa in His Vraja-entering form: He removes by approaching.
    • sa-balaḥ — with Balarāma
      Compound: sa (with) + Bala (Balarāma). Kṛṣṇa is named relationally — He is the One-with-Bala. In Gauḍīya theology, Balarāma is His ādi-guru and prakāśa; they are never seen apart in Vraja-līlā.
    • gopālaiḥ — with the cowherd boys
      Compound: go (cow) + pāla (protector). Both Kṛṣṇa and His friends are gopālas. The plural here is the sakhya-rasa community — the boys whose entire dharma is to be with Him.
    • vanam — the forest
      The Vṛndāvana forest. Gauḍīyas refuse to flatten 'forest' to scenery — vana is Vraja-dhāma itself, eternal in Goloka, manifest on earth at this very moment in the verse.
    • rantum — to enjoy (to sport)
      Infinitive of √ram — to play, to delight. The same root as rāsa. Kṛṣṇa enters to play; play is His default mode. Gauḍīyas insist this is not metaphor — līlā is His ontological mode.
    When the Vṛndāvana forest had thus become resplendent, filled with ripe dates and jambu fruits, Lord Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by His cows and cowherd boyfriends and accompanied by Śrī Balarāma, entered that forest to enjoy.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the Vṛndāvana forest had thus become resplendent, filled with ripe dates and jambu fruits, Lord Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by His cows and cowherd boyfriends and accompanied by Śrī Balarāma, entered that forest to enjoy.
    Commentary

    The description of the rainy season having been completed, now a description of Krsnas pastimes in the monsoon forests is described in seven verses. Krsna entered the forest of Vrnda which was flourishing (varsistham) with ripe date and jambu trees.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The monsoon having been described, now entering the forest for the Lord’s special pastimes-- the goal of the rains--is described. The word evam means “In the same way as I have described the monsoon I will describe Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes in the forest.” The cows and boys surrounded him in order to see the beauty of his face.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The monsoon having been described, now entering the forest for the Lord’s special pastimes-- the goal of the rains--is described. They entered the forest splendid with the rains just described (varṣiṣṭham) or resplendent with beauty. Though Vṛndāvana is the shelter of all seasons with a wealth of all flowers and fruits at all times, at this time the forest was even more abundant with dates and jambu fruits. Kṛṣṇa was surrounded by the boys because they wanted to protect him from the rain, each trying to cover him with their umbrella. The cows surrounded him with satisfaction, flowing with milk, having more affection for him than for their calves, as if offering him their milk. Attracting all minds (hariḥ), since he was surrounded by everyone, greedy for the beauty of his face, he entered the forest and remained there because of the beauty of the forest (pra-viśat). There is also the hint that he did this every day during the rainy season.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Vṛndāvana, ripe with dates and jambus, becomes the Lord's own playground: Kṛṣṇa enters surrounded by cows and friends, with Balarāma at His side. The whole long meditation on rain that the chapter has built converges on this one verse — the season existed to set this entry. Vraja is not background; it is the stage on which Bhagavān walks.

    Stories
    The cows recognising His call

    Across many chapters of Canto 10, Kṛṣṇa enters the forest with the herd and the cows know His call from any distance. Even when bewildered by Brahmā's theft of the calves (SB 10.13), the cows' bond holds. Their slow walk in v. 26 here is the same śāstric image of vātsalya-pulled motion.

    Gauḍīyas read v. 25 as the doorway: Bhagavān enters, and every creature of Vraja begins moving with Him. The whole chapter has been waiting for this verb — prāviśat.

    Important Words
    • prītyā — out of affection
      Instrumental of prīti — affection. Prīti is the standing word for Vaiṣṇava love in Gauḍīya theology (cf. Jīva Gosvāmī's Prīti-sandarbha). The cows are operating in prīti, not in habit.
    • snuta-stanāḥ — their teats wet (with milk)
      Compound: snuta (flowing) + stana (teat). Vātsalya is a bodily flow — the same compound-shape as putra-sneha-snuta in SB 10.9.3. The Bhāgavatam keeps showing love as something that leaks.
    • bhagavatā-āhūtāḥ — called by the Personality of Godhead
      Bhagavatā (instrumental) + āhūta (called). The cows hear Bhagavān's voice. Gauḍīyas note: His voice is direct in Vraja — no mediation needed. Cows hear it; the gopīs hear it; the flute calls and Vraja answers.
    • manda-gāminyaḥ — slow-going
      Compound: manda (slow) + gāminī (going). The cows' slowness is from love-weight, not weariness. Gauḍīyas distinguish: slowness from kleśa is bad, slowness from prema is the gopīs walking after Him at rāsa.
    • ūdhaḥ-bhāreṇa — by the weight of their milk-bags
      Compound: ūdhas (udder) + bhāra (weight). The body is heavy with what it has been making for Him. A perfect image for the heart of a sevā-doer.
    The cows had to move slowly because of their weighty milk bags, but they quickly ran to the Supreme Personality of Godhead as soon as He called them, their affection for Him causing their udders to become wet.
    Purport

    Śrīla Prabhupāda comments, “The cows, being fed by new grasses, became very healthy, and their milk bags were all very full. When Lord Kṛṣṇa called them by name, they immediately came to Him out of affection, and in their joyful condition the milk flowed from their bags.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The cows had to move slowly because of their weighty milk bags, but they quickly ran to the Supreme Personality of Godhead as soon as He called them, their affection for Him causing their udders to become wet.
    Commentary

    The milk flowed from the udders of the cows (snuta stanih) out of extreme motherly (vasalya) affection for Krsna.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The pastimes are described in six verses. Though the cows walked slowly, when called with affection they came quickly. As a symptom of their affection their udders dripped milk. Another version has snuta-stanīḥ. A particular glory of the monsoon season was the abundance of milk. The special prema arising between Kṛṣṇa and the cows in the presence of that abundance is shown with the cows participating in the pastimes.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The cows walk slowly under heavy udders, but the instant Kṛṣṇa calls they run — and their teats wet themselves with milk before any hand touches them. This is vātsalya in animal form. The body of a true bhakta does not need theological argument; the moment Bhagavān calls, the body itself begins to leak love.

    Stories
    The cows calling for their stolen calves

    When Brahmā stole the calves (SB 10.13), the cows refused grass and milk; their udders dried until Kṛṣṇa multiplied Himself into the missing calves. This verse is the joyful sister of that grief: same bond, opposite weather. Their milk flows toward Him whether He is present or absent.

    Gauḍīyas treasure these Vraja-cows as exemplars of vātsalya-bhakti even among non-human jīvas. Their bodies are bhakti-instruments — udders and feet and lowing all serve.

    Important Words
    • vana-okasaḥ — the forest-dwellers (aboriginal girls)
      Compound: vana (forest) + okasa (dweller). The pulinda women of Vraja. Gauḍīyas honour them: born outside varṇa-categories, they bear Kṛṣṇa-bhakti naturally — proof that bhakti is not constrained by birth.
    • madhu-cyutaḥ — dripping sweet sap
      Compound: madhu (honey, sweetness) + cyut (dropping). Vṛndāvana drips madhu in this season. The same word names Caitanya's poetry-line — madhu-rāja — and the gopīs' mood toward Kṛṣṇa (madhura).
    • vana-rājīḥ — rows of trees
      Compound: vana + rāji (row, line). The orderly avenues of Vraja's forest. Gauḍīyas note: even what looks wild in Vraja is arranged by yogamāyā for Kṛṣṇa's enjoyment.
    • guhāḥ — caves
      Plural of guhā. Vraja's caves shelter Kṛṣṇa in the rains (next verse). The Bhāgavatam uses guhā also for the cave of the heart — both shelters of the Lord.
    • jala-dhārāḥ — waterfalls
      Compound: jala (water) + dhārā (stream). The waterfalls' sound — the verse explicitly notes — tells Kṛṣṇa where caves are. Sound is sākṣāt evidence. Vraja's geography speaks.
    The Lord saw the joyful aborigine girls of the forest, the trees dripping sweet sap, and the mountain waterfalls, whose resounding indicated that there were caves nearby.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Lord saw the joyful aborigine girls of the forest, the trees dripping sweet sap, and the mountain waterfalls, whose resounding indicated that there were caves nearby.
    Commentary

    In the monsoon forests Krsna saw the joyful pulinda women. He saw honey flowing from the trees, waterfalls flowing from the mountains, and far off caves, which appeared to be close from the echoing sound.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Vanaukasaḥ refers to Pulindas and others. He saw caves because they were indicated by echoes, even though they were far away and covered by grass. Dadṛśe means dadarṣa.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa, walking in His own forest, takes in the joyful pulinda-girls, the sweet-sap-dripping trees and the cave-echoing waterfalls. Even He, who saw everything before time began, gladly looks. Gauḍīyas read the verse closely: the Lord delights in Vraja's particular details, which means Vraja's details are not optional decoration but His own internal potency manifesting outward.

    Important Words
    • reme — He enjoyed (played)
      Aorist of √ram — He delighted. The same root as in v. 25's rantum. The Lord's purpose in the forest is reme — to play. Gauḍīyas refuse functionalist explanations: He plays because He is Kṛṣṇa.
    • bhagavān — the Supreme Personality of Godhead
      The full name for Kṛṣṇa as svayaṁ-bhagavān (SB 1.3.28). The verse uses the loftiest title and then describes Him eating tubers in a cave — the Bhāgavatam's signature juxtaposition.
    • kanda-mūla-phala-aśanaḥ — eating roots, tubers and fruits
      Long compound: kanda (root) + mūla (tuber) + phala (fruit) + aśana (eating). Renunciate diet, taken by the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha for the joy of being in Vraja. The diet is vrata, the mood is mādhurya.
    • guhāyām — in a cave
      Locative. The same guhā as v. 27. Gauḍīyas note: the same cave that hides Kṛṣṇa from the rain is the cave-of-heart that hides Him from non-devotees. Both shelters.
    • vanaspati-kroḍe — in the hollow of a tree
      Compound: vanaspati (lord of the forest, a fruiting tree) + kroḍa (cavity, lap). Tree-as-lap — the forest cradles Bhagavān. Gauḍīyas hear vātsalya from the forest itself: Vṛndāvana is a mother.
    When it rained, the Lord would sometimes enter a cave or the hollow of a tree to play and to eat roots and fruits.
    Purport

    Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī explains that during the rainy season bulbs and roots are very tender and palatable, and Lord Kṛṣṇa would eat them along with wild fruits found in the forest. Lord Kṛṣṇa and His young boyfriends would sit in the hollow of a tree or within a cave and enjoy pastimes while waiting for the rain to stop.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When it rained, the Lord would sometimes enter a cave or the hollow of a tree to play and to eat roots and fruits.
    Commentary

    When it rained all around (abhi varsati) Krsna would run and enter the hollow of a tree or a cave and amuse himself by eating radish. There are two types of radish: round ones and long ones.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kvacit means sometimes or in some places. Though he was the Supreme Lord he ate the forest roots and fruits. See the sweetness of his pastimes! Kanda are round roots and mūla are long. They are mentioned before the fruit because they were most excellent, being soft in the monsoon season.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kvacit means sometimes or in some places. Either in the cave or in holes of trees (ca) he would play and eat fruits. Or by his powers he would go at the same time into the cave and into the hole of the tree because he was bhagavān. He did this sometimes when it rained profusely (abhivarṣati). In his human pastimes he showed his special nature as bhagavān by this power. The caves and holes in the trees were similar, having broad areas. Some other boys would also sometimes be there. He played there or was happy there (reme). Why? He ate roots (kaṇdā and mūla) which can be distinguished by external and internal differences. During the monsoon they were suitable because they were plentiful and soft. The fruits were previously described (dates and jambu).

    Related values & verses
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    When the rain falls, the Lord steps into a hollow tree or a cave and eats roots and fruits, playing all the while. Gauḍīyas linger on this verse: the Supreme, who has the universe for a stomach, eats kanda-mūla in a Vraja-cave because His friends are eating it. Mādhurya means He shrinks to share the menu of those He loves.

    Stories
    Eating leaves with Vidura, eating fruits with the boys

    When Kṛṣṇa visited Vidura, He ate leafy vegetables prepared with love and refused the rich fare offered by Duryodhana (Mahābhārata, Udyoga-parva). The same logic: the Lord eats what His devotee can give. Here in Vraja the boys eat fruits and roots; He eats fruits and roots.

    Gauḍīyas read SB 10.20.28 as the structural twin of the Vidura episode. The Lord's plate is set by His devotee's heart, not by His own appetite.

    Important Words
    • dadhi-odanam — rice mixed with yogurt
      Compound: dadhi (yogurt) + odana (boiled rice). The most homely meal of Vraja. Gauḍīyas treasure dadhi-odana as Kṛṣṇa's affection-food — what mothers send from home. Caitanya's cīḍā-dadhi feast is its descendant.
    • saṅkarṣaṇa-anvitaḥ — accompanied by Saṅkarṣaṇa (Balarāma)
      Compound: Saṅkarṣaṇa (one who draws together — Balarāma) + anvita (accompanied). Saṅkarṣaṇa is Balarāma's expansion-name in the catur-vyūha. The brothers eat side by side; this is the picture Gauḍīyas hold.
    • salila-antike — near the water
      Compound: salila (water) + antika (near). Probably the Yamunā. The picnic-spot is precisely placed; Gauḍīyas remember that every detail of Vraja has been identified by the Six Gosvāmīs.
    • sambhojanīyaiḥ — with those who regularly ate with Him
      From sam + √bhuj — co-eaters. There is a named set of boys who share Kṛṣṇa's plate. Sakhya-rasa is structurally about co-eating; the verse marks the technical category.
    • śīlāyām — on a flat stone
      Locative of śilā — slab, stone. Vraja's many flat rocks are līlā-furniture. Govardhana itself becomes one; here a smaller cousin serves as table.
    Lord Kṛṣṇa would take His meal of boiled rice and yogurt, sent from home, in the company of Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa and the cowherd boys who regularly ate with Him. They would all sit down to eat on a large stone near the water.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Kṛṣṇa would take His meal of boiled rice and yogurt, sent from home, in the company of Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa and the cowherd boys who regularly ate with Him. They would all sit down to eat on a large stone near the water.
    Commentary

    People from his house brought food to a place called "Chak" . Krsna sat on a stone slab near the water. Even today people can see that eating place on the bank of a kunda.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He took food brought by his relatives, or brought by friends who were nearby. He ate with cowherds who were qualified to eat with him, being similar in nature (saṁbhojanīyaiḥ). Sam means together. Or saṁbhojanīyaiḥ it can mean “together with condiments.” Balarāma was in their midst.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The food brought with them, packed by Yaśodā, was brought close by the boys at the appropriate time or was offered by each of them as a gift to Kṛṣṇa (samānītam), because it was plentiful and sweet. He ate on a stone plate, since the food was liquid with plentiful yogurt and because the stone became beautiful after being cleansed by the showers. He ate near the water. In that season there was water everywhere. Or he chose a spot near the water in order to drink water. He had all the boys eat, since they ate together on one stone plate. He made them sit down in one place. Balarāma made them come together as one (saṅkarṣaṇa) since the two boys were not separate from the other cowherds. Or śīlāyām in the singular can mean many stone plates since there was not enough room on one plate. Kṛṣṇa made the boys sit in rows, putting Balarāma in the center, and personally served the food and made them eat. Then he ate.

    Analogy

    On a flat stone by the water Kṛṣṇa eats yogurt-rice with His brother and the cowherd boys — the most ordinary picnic in the world, set in the middle of the Bhāgavatam. Sakhya-rasa lives in this verse. The Lord of all sacrifices accepts dadhi-odana from a friend's tiffin and eats sitting on a rock; no greater śloka has ever been needed to define the highest theology.

    Stories
    Caitanya at Pāṇihāṭi, the cīḍā-dadhi feast

    Nityānanda Prabhu, dancing at Pāṇihāṭi, asked Raghunātha dāsa to feed everyone cīḍā and dadhi — and the Lord Himself ate alongside (Caitanya-caritāmṛta, Antya 6). The mood was exactly SB 10.20.29 — flat ground, simple food, friends in a circle, Bhagavān at the centre.

    Gauḍīyas treat Pāṇihāṭi as the rebirth of this Vraja-verse. The picnic on the stone never ended; it moved to a riverbank in Bengal.

    Important Words
    • ātma-śakti-upabṛṁhitām — expanded from His own internal potency
      Compound: ātma (own) + śakti (potency) + upabṛṁhita (expanded). The Gauḍīya doctrine of līlā-śakti in one phrase: the seasons of Vraja are not foreign material but Bhagavān's own internal energy taking outward form. Vraja's monsoon is His; He greets it as His own.
    • sarva-kāla-sukha-āvahām — perennial source of great happiness
      Compound: sarva (all) + kāla (time) + sukha (happiness) + āvaha (bearing). The 'happiness for all time' — because, Gauḍīyas note, Vraja is eternal in Goloka; what looks seasonal is in fact unending.
    • pūjayām cakre — He offered respect
      Periphrastic perfect of √pūj — He performed pūjā. The verb is precise: Bhagavān worships. He pūjās His own potency, modelling for jīvas the gesture even where He alone is the addressee.
    • śādvala-upari — on the green grass
      Compound: śādvala (lawn of new grass) + upari (upon). The exact texture of Vraja's monsoon turf. Gauḍīyas treasure these specifics — the dhāma is detailed, not generic.
    • tṛptān — contented
      From √tṛp — to be satisfied. The bulls are tṛpta — eyes shut, fully fed. The same word names the bhakta's heart when he has had darśana. The grass and the darśana achieve the same internal state.
    • mīlita-īkṣaṇān — with closed eyes
      Compound: mīlita (closed) + īkṣaṇa (eye). The bulls close their eyes from satisfaction — a small image of samādhi in cattle. Gauḍīyas love such a detail: even bovine peace is a face of Kṛṣṇa's mercy.
    Lord Kṛṣṇa watched the contented bulls, calves and cows sitting on the green grass and grazing with closed eyes, and He saw that the cows were tired from the burden of their heavy milk bags. Thus observing the beauty and opulence of Vṛndāvana’s rainy season, a perennial source of great happiness, the Lord offered all respect to that season, which was expanded from His own internal potency.
    Purport

    The lush beauty of the rainy season in Vṛndāvana is meant to enhance the pleasure pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Thus, to set the scene for the Lord’s loving affairs, His internal potency makes all the arrangements described in this chapter.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Kṛṣṇa watched the contented bulls, calves and cows sitting on the green grass and grazing with closed eyes, and He saw that the cows were tired from the burden of their heavy milk bags. Thus observing the beauty and opulence of Vṛndāvana's rainy season, a perennial source of great happiness, the Lord offered all respect to that season, which was expanded from His own internal potency.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He saw the cows, bulls and calves sitting on green pastures, with eyes closed, ruminating (carvataḥ). The season was surcharged with the hlādini-śakti (ātma-śakti) which made the season qualified for his pastimes. He considered the season proper (pūjayām cakre). unmatta-śikhi-sāraṅge tasmin kāle mahāvane / kṛṣṇarāmau mudāyuktau gopālaiś ceratuḥ saha // kvicid gobhiḥ samaṁ ramyaṁ geya-tāla-ratā bubhau / ceratuḥ kvacid atyarthaṁ śīta-vṛkṣa-talāśritau // kvacit kadaṁba-srak-citrau mayūra-srag-virājitau / viliptau kvacid āsātāṁ vividhair giri-dhātubhiḥ // parṇaśayyāsu saṁsuptau kvacin nidrāntaraiṣiṇau / kvacid garjati jīmūte hāhā-kāra-ravākulau // Surrounded by cowherd boys, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma wandered in the large forest during the monsoon, filled with impassioned peacocks and cātaka birds. Sometimes they would sing as they wandered in the forests made beautiful by the cows. They would sit at the bases of cool trees. They were decorated in kadamba garlands and garlands made of peacock feathers. Sometimes they would decorate themselves with various minerals from the mountains. Sometimes they would sleep on beds made of leaves and after sleep would desire to play again. Sometimes when the clouds rumbled they would shout. Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.6.44-47

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He saw the cows ruminating and the beauty of the season. The animals were sitting because they were satisfied (tṛptān). During the monsoon, there was plentiful soft grass everywhere. In one place, in one moment they could fill their stomachs. The word ca indicates the whole group. They sat near Kṛṣṇa. The cows also sat because their udders were full. The cows and bulls are mentioned because they were in the majority, but buffalos were also present. He saw the beauty of the monsoon with the forests, which was previously described (tām). Or he saw the beauty of the monsoon which was indescribable (tām). Beauty of the monsoon means beauty of the forest, deer and buffaloes in the monsoon season. Megha-prṣṭhe balākānāṁ rarāja vimalā tatiḥ Durvṛtter vṛtta-ceṣṭeva kulīnasyātiśobhanā A spotless line of cranes shone on the surface of a cloud. The well-bred were splendid and the wicked were futile in their actions. Viṣṇu Purāṇa The monsoon season was filled with the Lord’ṣ śakti in the form of time. This made it different. Time serves the Lord. Or though it was filled with his own powers (ātma-śakty-upabṛṁhitām) he praised it with affection (pūjayām cakre) or thought it excellent, because it gave happiness to all beings continuously. Instead of sukha sometimes mudā is seen with the same meaning. Or one may worry that the swans would be suffering. The season was endowed with the Lord’s power so that even they were happy. Other pastimes are described by Parāśara: unmatta-śikhi-sāraṅge tasmin kāle mahāvane / kṛṣṇarāmau mudāyuktau gopālaiś ceratuḥ saha // kvicid gobhiḥ samaṁ ramyaṁ geya-tāla-ratā bubhau / ceratuḥ kvacid atyarthaṁ śīta-vṛkṣa-talāśritau // kvacit kadaṁba-srak-citrau mayūra-srag-virājitau / viliptau kvacid āsātāṁ vividhair giri-dhātubhiḥ // parṇaśayyāsu saṁsuptau kvacin nidrāntaraiṣiṇau / kvacid garjati jīmūte hāhā-kāra-ravākulau // Surrounded by cowherd boys, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma wandered in the large forest during the monsoon, filled with impassioned peacocks and cātaka birds. Sometimes they would sing as they wandered in the forests made beautiful by the cows. They would sit at the bases of cool trees. They were decorated with kadamba garlands and garlands made of peacock feathers. Sometimes they would decorate themselves with various minerals from the mountains. Sometimes they would sleep on beds made of leaves and after sleep would desire to play again. Sometimes when the clouds rumbled they would shout. Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.6.44-47

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa, watching contented bulls graze with closed eyes and cows tired by milk-weight, offers respect to the very rainy season — for it is His own internal potency expanded outward. The verse is the chapter's deep secret: He worships His own śakti. The world is not external to Him; ātma-śakti is what He sees, and He bows to it.

    Important Words
    • śarat — autumn
      The classical season-name. Śarat is Vraja's rāsa-season — chapters 29–33 of this canto. The whole second half of this chapter is structurally a prelude to the rāsa-līlā. Gauḍīyas read it as such.
    • rāma-keśavayoḥ — of Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa
      Dvandva genitive dual. Keśava — the Lord of beautiful hair, or the slayer of Keśī, or He who has Brahmā and Śiva as His Ka and Īśa. Gauḍīyas treasure Keśava as a Vraja-specific name (the Keśī-slaying is Vraja-līlā).
    • svaccha-ambu — with clear water
      Compound: svaccha (clear, transparent) + ambu (water). The water that has settled. Gauḍīyas note: a settled mind is svaccha — Kṛṣṇa is seen in it as in autumn-clear water.
    • aparuṣa-anilā — with gentle wind
      Compound: a-paruṣa (not harsh) + anila (wind). Vraja's autumn wind is mild. Gauḍīyas read this as the wind that will, soon, carry the flute-sound to the gopīs' houses.
    • vyabhrā — cloudless
      Vy + abhra (cloud). Without clouds. The contrast with the chapter's opening is deliberate: from sky-covered-by-clouds to sky-cleared. Kṛṣṇa has not changed; the sky has.
    While Lord Rāma and Lord Keśava were thus dwelling in Vṛndāvana, the fall season arrived, when the sky is cloudless, the water clear and the wind gentle.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    While Lord Rāma and Lord Keśava were thus dwelling in Vṛndāvana, the fall season arrived, when the sky is cloudless, the water clear and the wind gentle.
    Commentary

    Here begins the description of the autumn season in eight verses. In the autumn season the water became clear, the wind became peaceful.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma lived with great attachment (ni—vasatoḥ) in Vraja, with special pastimes in the monsoon season. Autumn then made its appearance with special treasures (sam—abhavat).

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The autumn arrives — cloudless sky, clear water, soft wind — and the Vraja-stage is reset for the rāsa to come. The chapter has been moving toward this. After the rain has done its long descriptive work, the season turns crystalline, and Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma keep dwelling in Vraja under a different sky.

    Important Words
    • yoga-niṣevayā — by the practice of yoga
      Compound: yoga + niṣevā (close practice). In Gauḍīya reading, the highest yoga is bhakti-yoga (Gītā 6.47 — yoginām api sarveṣāṁ). The verse's 'yoga' is read as bhakti-yoga's return.
    • bhraṣṭānām — of those who have fallen
      Past participle genitive plural — of the fallen. Bhakti's particular generosity: it names fall (bhraṣṭa) and offers re-entry. Gauḍīyas read this verse alongside Gītā 6.40 — na hi kalyāṇa-kṛt kaścid durgatiṁ tāta gacchati.
    • prakṛtim-yayuḥ — returned to their original nature
      Prakṛti here = svarūpa, original nature. Gauḍīyas note: the jīva's prakṛti is dāsya/sakhya/vātsalya/mādhurya with Kṛṣṇa, not formless brahmatva. The verse hints that bhakti returns the soul to its true relational shape.
    • nīraja-utpattyā — by the regeneration of lotuses
      Compound: nīra-ja (water-born = lotus) + utpatti (arising). The lotus regenerates with the autumn. Kṛṣṇa's eyes and feet are lotus-like; autumn is iconographic Vraja-season.
    • cetāṁsi — minds
      Plural of cetas — mind, consciousness. The same word as v. 14's cittam (cognate). The yogīs' minds, like the lakes, are cleansed. Gauḍīyas distinguish citta-śuddhi (a mental result) from bhāva (a heart-condition produced by bhakti).
    The autumn season, which regenerated the lotus flowers, also restored the various bodies of water to their original purity, just as the process of devotional service purifies the minds of the fallen yogīs when they return to it.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The autumn season, which regenerated the lotus flowers, also restored the various bodies of water to their original purity, just as the process of devotional service purifies the minds of the fallen yogīs when they return to it.
    Commentary

    Because of the autumn season, during which the lotuses bloomed, the waters became clear, just like by practice of bhakti seva the heart becomes purified and the lord appears. The autumn season is compared to the bhakti seva, the lake to the heart, and the appearance of Krsna is compared to the lotus. This is a positive example.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The water became clear with the arrival of autumn when lotuses bloomed. This meaning, of the two alternatives offered by Śrīdhara Svāmī, is acceptable.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The minds of those who have fallen from yoga because of obstacles and are impure become pure again by practice of yoga. The lotus helps the water become pure.

      His Holiness Vrindavan Chandra Das Goswami· 2023-10-28· Hindi
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Autumn regenerates the lotuses and clears the lakes — as the practice of bhakti, returning, cleans the minds of fallen yogīs. The verse is generous to lapsed sādhakas: prakṛtim yayuḥ — they return to their original nature. There is no permanent fall in Bhāgavatam-theology. The lake forgets the rain; the soul forgets the slip.

    Stories
    Bharata's return through three lives

    Mahārāja Bharata fell from his bhakti by attachment to a deer, was born a deer, then a brāhmaṇa as Jaḍa-Bharata — and finally taught Rahūgaṇa King the highest jñāna-bhakti (SB 5.7–14). His prakṛti returned, slowly, through grace. The verse's metaphor is his story.

    Gauḍīyas insist on this generosity. No fall is final for one who began as a yogī; bhakti's autumn always comes again.
